## Executive Summary: 2026 Colorado River Guidelines and Lower-Basin Cutbacks

## S.1 Problem Context

The Colorado River Basin confronts a structural supply–demand deficit of unprecedented magnitude, driven by a 25-year megadrought in which **20 of the past 25 years** have produced below-average inflows into Lake Powell. The Bureau of Reclamation's August 2025 24-Month Study projects a January 1, 2026, Lake Mead elevation of **1,055.88 feet**—a level that triggers the most severe shortage-tier operations contemplated under the existing 2007 Interim Guidelines and the 2019 Drought Contingency Plan (DCP). Absent intervention, Glen Canyon Dam releases would fall below the **7.48 MAF** annual minimum, and Hoover Dam deliveries would be curtailed across the Lower Basin, imposing uncompensated economic losses on agricultural, municipal, and tribal water users in California, Arizona, Nevada, and Mexico.

## S.2 Key Systems and Governance Architecture

The 2026 allocation framework is defined by three interlocking instruments: (i) the **May 2023 Lower Basin States Agreement**, in which Arizona, California, and Nevada committed to conserve **at least 3.0 MAF** by end of calendar year 2026, with **≥1.5 MAF** delivered by end of 2024 ; (ii) the **Near-Term Colorado River Operations Draft Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement (Draft SEIS)** process, which incorporates the Lower Basin Plan as an action alternative; and (iii) the binational **IBWC Treaty framework**, under which Mexico's Water Reserve can offset U.S. cutbacks via water creation or delivery from the U.S. side.
